# Numbers 23 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Structure Overview

The chapter falls into four sections: the first prophecy (vv. 1–10), the relocation (vv. 11–17), the second prophecy (vv. 18–24), and a further relocation (vv. 25–30). Chapters 23–24 contain seven oracles of Balaam (introduced at 23:7a, 23:18a; 24:3a, 24:15a, 24:20b, 24:21b, 24:23a). — Precept Austin (citing NET Notes and Allen, EBC); https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-23-commentary

---

## v. 1 — "Build for me seven altars here, and prepare for me seven bulls and seven rams."

**Traditional Readings**

- **Seven altars as pagan ritual:** Nowhere in Scripture is more than one altar mentioned for the worship of Yahweh. The seven altars and sacrifices have the earmarks of pagan magic, not the worship prescribed in the Tabernacle. — Precept Austin (citing Allen, EBC); https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-23-commentary

- **God never commanded this:** Balaam sought to turn Yahweh against Israel; the seven altars and sacrifices were intended to appease the LORD. But God never told Balaam to build an altar, much less seven. These were Balaam and Balak's idea, not God's. — Enduring Word (David Guzik); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Calvin's view:** Balaam was infected by the superstitious notion that the number seven held secret power, common among pagans. He "borrowed devices in various directions, which savored of nothing but the illusions of the devil." Calvin warns that superstitious people "neither spare expense, nor refuse anything which is demanded by the masters of their errors." — Calvin's Commentary; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

- **Ellicott:** The patriarchs never erected more than one altar in one place; a plurality of altars was the badge of idolatry. The number seven was regarded as significant among Greeks and Romans as well as Israelites. — Ellicott (from search excerpt); https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/23.htm

- **Pulpit Commentary:** According to the common opinion of the heathen, it was necessary to propitiate with sacrifices the God with whom they had to do. The number seven was especially connected with the revelation of the true God, the Creator. The sacrifices were offered, no doubt, to Jehovah. — Pulpit Commentary (from search excerpt); https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-23.html

- **Constable:** Pagans as well as Israelites regarded seven as a complete number based on the seven days of creation. Pagans commonly offered sacrifices on important occasions to secure divine favour. — Constable; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-23.html

- **Milgrom (Jewish scholarship, cited by Precept Austin):** The magical use of seven is widely attested in the Bible: Naaman bathes seven times (2 Kings 5:10), Elijah's servant scans seven times (1 Kings 18:43), Joshua circuits Jericho seven times (Josh 6:4). The many animals would provide abundant liver and organ materials for the diviner. — Precept Austin; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-23-commentary

---

## v. 2 — "So Balak did as Balaam had instructed, and Balak and Balaam offered a bull and a ram on each altar."

- **Ellicott** notes it is more probable that Balak, as a king, performed priestly functions than that Balaam performed them alone (see also Num 22:40). — Ellicott (from search excerpt); https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/23.htm

- These were not the sacrifices Yahweh prescribed in Numbers 15 but pagan sacrifices. — Precept Austin; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-23-commentary

---

## v. 3 — "Stay here by your burnt offering while I am gone … Perhaps the LORD will meet with me … So Balaam went off to a barren height."

- **"To a barren height" (שֶׁפִי, shephi):** The Hebrew term is debated. It can mean "a bare hill," "a solitary place," "a desolate height," or "a high place." Hengstenberg adopts "bare hill," since the root verb means "to plane or smooth off." — Precept Austin (citing Bush and Hengstenberg); https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-23-commentary

- **Augury background:** Balaam was an augur by profession, foretelling the future based on omens from nature. He went to a bare height where he might see omens. Numbers 24:1 confirms this: "he did not go as at other times to seek omens." — Precept Austin (citing Jensen and Bush); https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-23-commentary

- **Calvin:** Balaam here imitates the true servants of God by seeking retirement, since God almost always appeared to His servants when they were separated from the crowd. But there was no sincerity in him. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Balaam went to look for "auguries" — natural signs in the flight of birds and the like that the heathen observed. But from the fact that God *met* him (v. 4), we may conclude Balaam's words meant more than mere augury. — Pulpit (from search excerpt); https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-23.html

---

## v. 4 — "And God met with him. 'I have set up seven altars,' Balaam said, 'and on each altar I have offered a bull and a ram.'"

- **God meets a sorcerer:** This is remarkable. God met with someone as corrupt as Balaam. Spiritual giftedness does not equal spiritual maturity or holiness of life. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Calvin:** "It is wonderful that God should have determined to have anything in common with the pollutions of Balaam; since there is no communion between light and darkness." God's meeting him was by no means a sign of approval of the seven altars. God "well knows how to apply corrupt instruments to His use." — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

- **Allen (cited by Constable and Enduring Word):** "Despite the pagan and unsavory actions of this ungodly man, the Lord deigns to meet with him and to speak through him. … God may use whatever vessel he wishes; the issue concerns what happens to an unclean vessel when God has finished using it for his purposes." — Constable; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-23.html

- **Bishop Hall (cited by Precept Austin):** "But will God meet with a sorcerer? … O man, who shall prescribe God what instruments he shall use! He knows how to employ, not only saints and angels, but wicked men, beasts, devils, to his own glory." — Precept Austin; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-23-commentary

- Balaam boasts of his seven altars as if he had duly propitiated God. Thus hypocrites arrogantly trust they deserve well of God when they only provoke Him. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

---

## v. 5 — "Then the LORD put a message in Balaam’s mouth, saying, 'Return to Balak and give him this message.'"

- **"Put a word in Balaam's mouth":** God spoke through someone as ungodly as Balaam — just as He had spoken through a donkey in the previous chapter. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Bishop Wordsworth (cited by Ellicott):** "God, who had opened the mouth of the ass, in a manner contrary to her nature, now opens Balaam's mouth in a manner contrary to his own will." — Ellicott (from search excerpt); https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/23.htm

- **Trapp (cited by Enduring Word):** "The words thus put into his mouth, do but pass from him; they are not polluted by him, because they are not his! … Balaam did not 'eat' God's word as Jeremiah did (Jer 15:16)." — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Calvin:** The holy Prophets spoke from the heart the treasures God had deposited with them; Balaam's case was different — his mind was alienated while he delivered the words put into his mouth. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

---

## vv. 7–10 — Balaam's First Oracle

### v. 7 — "And Balaam lifted up an oracle, saying: 'Balak brought me from Aram … Come, put a curse on Jacob for me …'"

- **"Took up his oracle" (מָשָׁל, mashal):** The word signifies weighty, notable sayings expressed in exalted, poetic language. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

- **Aram:** Refers to Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates (cf. Paddan-aram, Gen 28:2). — Constable; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-23.html. Calvin notes that Aram/Syria here refers to the region contiguous to Arabia toward the Red Sea, not distant Mesopotamia. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

### v. 8 — "How can I curse what God has not cursed? How can I denounce what the LORD has not denounced?"

- Balaam or any prophet could not curse Israel if God had not cursed them. Balak could not bribe God. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Meyer (cited by Enduring Word):** "Balaam would have reversed the blessing into a curse, had he been able. … Is not this also the despair of Satan? God hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in Christ Jesus, and he cannot reverse them." — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Calvin:** Balaam confesses his tongue was tied so that he could not utter a single syllable against God's command. Balak's assumption that Balaam possessed the power to curse or bless at will was "to depose God from His supremacy." — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

### v. 9 — "Behold, a people dwelling apart, not reckoning themselves among the nations."

- **Separateness of Israel:** Israel was different from all other nations, chosen by God for His unfolding plan of redemption. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Calvin:** "The people shall dwell alone" means they shall be content with their own condition, neither desiring the wealth of others nor seeking their aid. "Not reckoned among the nations" is not depreciation but exaltation — no nation is comparable with them because of God's adoption. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

- **Clarke (cited by Enduring Word):** "They shall ever be preserved as a distinct nation. This prophecy has been literally fulfilled through a period of 3300 years to the present day. This is truly astonishing." — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Constable:** Israel was not reckoned among the nations "because of her divine vocation in the earth that set her apart from all other peoples." — Constable; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-23.html

- **Pulpit Homiletics** sees this as deeply true of the redeemed people of God in every age: "The same grand distinction belongs to all whom Christ has redeemed from among men." — Biblehub Homiletics; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/23.htm

### v. 10 — "Who can count the dust of Jacob or number even a fourth of Israel? Let me die the death of the righteous; let my end be like theirs!"

- **"Dust of Jacob":** A clear reference to God's promise to Abraham (Gen 13:16). — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **"Fourth part of Israel":** Refers to the quarter of the camp closest to Balaam. He could not even count the nearest quarter. — Constable; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-23.html

- **"Let me die the death of the righteous":** Balaam longed to die the death of the righteous but had no desire to live the life of the righteous. His actual death (Num 31:8) gives no hope for the fulfilment of this wish. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Poole (cited by Enduring Word):** Israel has the peculiar privilege of being happy after death; their happiness begins where other people's ends. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Trapp (cited by Enduring Word):** "They would break God's chain, sunder happiness from holiness, salvation from sanctification … dance with the devil all day, and then sup with Christ at night." — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Spurgeon (cited by Enduring Word):** "Behold the vanity of mere desires. Balaam desired to die the death of the righteous, and yet was slain in battle fighting against those righteous men whom he envied." — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Calvin** sees this as a testimony to future immortality: Balaam unwittingly confessed that God's grace extends beyond this life. The Israelites are called "righteous" not on account of their own righteousness but because of God's good pleasure in separating them. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

---

## vv. 11–12 — Balak's First Disappointment

### v. 11 — "What have you done to me? I brought you here to curse my enemies, and behold, you have only blessed them!"

- The king of Moab was understandably disturbed. He paid good money for a curse and got blessing instead. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

### v. 12 — "Should I not speak exactly what the LORD puts in my mouth?"

- Balaam spoke as a true prophet yet a corrupt prophet. He was disappointed he couldn't please the king who promised him riches. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Calvin:** Balaam is compelled to repress Balak's "stupid arrogance" by pleading God's command. He acted the part of a true prophet in words, though his feelings were altogether on the other side. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

---

## vv. 13–17 — Relocation to Pisgah

### v. 13 — "Please come with me to another place where you can see them. You will only see the outskirts … And from there, curse them for me."

- Balak hoped changing Balaam's perspective would change the prophecy. Since Balaam seemed impressed by Israel's size (v. 10), Balak placed him where he could see only a portion. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Calvin:** Balak did what superstitious people do — carried about from one speculation to another, trying now this, now that. They imagined magical power in the gaze of the enchanter. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

### v. 14 — "the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah"

- **Pisgah:** The same ridge from which Moses would later view the Promised Land (Deut 34:1). Zophim means "watchers" or "spies," likely named for its position as a lookout. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

### vv. 15–17 — Repeated sacrifice and God's meeting

- Balak was willing to build seven more altars and supply more sacrifices. Once again Balaam could only speak what God put in his mouth. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Calvin:** Balak's inquiry "What did the LORD say?" shows hypocrisy: "Thus do hypocrites profess anxious solicitude in inquiring the will of God, whilst the knowledge of it is intolerable to them." — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

---

## vv. 18–24 — Balaam's Second Oracle

### v. 18 — "Arise, O Balak, and listen; give ear to me, O son of Zippor."

- The repetition ("Arise … listen; give ear to me") is emphatic and indicates something extraordinary. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

### v. 19 — "God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind. Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill?"

This is the theological centre of the chapter, widely cited across traditions.

**Reformed / Baptist (John Piper):**
- God's commitment to His promises hangs on His not repenting like a man. God can foresee all circumstances; nothing will occur that causes Him to take back His promises. When the Bible elsewhere says God "repents" (e.g., 1 Sam 15:11), it means God's "repentance" is not like man's — not from ignorance of the future. God expresses a different attitude because changed circumstances make a different expression fitting, though He foresaw it all. — John Piper, Desiring God; https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-does-not-repent-like-a-man

**Reformed (Calvin):**
- Men lie because they are fickle, changeable, or unable to accomplish what they promised. None of this applies to God: He is neither deceived, nor deceives, nor has any "shadow of turning" (James 1:17). The point is that God is unchangeable in what He has decreed — "His election … is without repentance." — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):**
- God cannot be bribed or impressed with riches (as Balaam was). He does not lie, does not change His mind as man does, always performs His word, and has the power to perform what He promises. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

**Evangelical (Constable):**
- God does not change His ultimate purposes or go back on His solemn promises. He does respond to people's actions by adjusting His plans, but from His larger purposes He does not "repent." The point is that God is not fickle; no one can induce Him to curse those He has chosen to bless. — Constable; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-23.html

**Baptist (Gill, via search excerpt):**
- Man goes astray from the womb speaking lies, but God cannot lie. His counsels are faithfulness and truth, His promises are yea and amen in Christ. Repentance belongs to men who change their minds because something unforeseen happens; nothing of this kind can befall God. — Gill (search excerpt); https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/23-19.html

### v. 20 — "I have indeed received a command to bless; He has blessed, and I cannot change it."

- It was not within Balaam's power to bless or curse Israel; he could only report what God said. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Cole (cited by Enduring Word):** "God's blessing is so powerful and irrevocable that even the most renowned divination expert of the day could not counter its effectiveness." — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

### v. 21 — "He considers no disaster for Jacob; He sees no trouble for Israel. The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of the King is among them."

- **"No iniquity in Jacob":** At this time Israel was not walking in flagrant sin, so under the Mosaic covenant they were in a position of blessing. However, this also hinted at a dark principle: if Israel could be enticed into sin, they might bring a curse on themselves — which is exactly what Balaam later advised (Num 25, 31:16). — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Poole (cited by Enduring Word):** "For as Balaam knew that none but Israel's God could curse or destroy Israel, so he knew that nothing but their sin could move him so to do; and therefore he took a right, though wicked, course afterwards to tempt them to sin." — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **"The shout of the King":** This is the first specific mention of Yahweh as King among His people in Scripture. — Enduring Word (citing Poole); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **Constable:** "He has not observed misfortune [iniquity] in Jacob" means not that Israel was sinless, but their sins were not sufficient to change God's ultimate purpose to bless her. — Constable; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-23.html

### v. 22 — "God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox."

- **Verb tense:** The Hebrew verb describes ongoing action — God delivered them and *continues* to deliver them. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

- **"Wild ox" (רְאֵם, reem):** The KJV translates "unicorn," but this is misleading. The Hebrew word occurs nine times in the OT and likely refers to a wild ox, rhinoceros, or buffalo. Some see it as a two-horned creature (the Hebrew has a dual form). — Enduring Word (citing Allen and Clarke); https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/ and Precept Austin; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-23-commentary

### v. 23 — "For there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel."

- **Traditional translation (KJV, ESV, etc.):** No sorcery or divination can succeed *against* Israel. Balaam confesses his arts are powerless against God's protected people. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

- **Alternative translation (Ellicott, Hengstenberg):** The verse may be rendered "For there is no augury *in* Jacob, and there is no divination *in* Israel." The Israelites had no need of augury and divination because God revealed His acts, counsel, and will directly to them through prophets and Urim and Thummim. — Ellicott (from search excerpt); https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/23.htm

- **Gill** notes both interpretations: (1) no enchantment avails against Israel; (2) there are no enchanters or diviners *among* Israel — they are fit for blessing because they don't practice these things. — Gill (from search excerpt); https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/23-23.htm

- **Hengstenberg (cited by Ellicott):** "What is here affirmed of Israel applies to the Church of all ages, and also to every individual believer. The Church of God knows from His own Word what God does … The wisdom of this world resembles augury and divination." — Ellicott (from search excerpt); https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/23.htm

- **"What great things God has done!":** This will be the amazed testimony concerning Israel in every age. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

### v. 24 — "Behold, the people rise like a lioness … not resting until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain."

- Balaam transfers to the whole nation what Jacob had prophesied of Judah in Genesis 49:9. — Ellicott (from search excerpt); https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/23.htm

- **Calvin:** The comparison does not signify cruelty or rapaciousness, but boldness, strength, and promptness in resistance. The sum is that however Israel might be attacked, it would be endued with invincible fortitude. — Calvin; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-23.html

- **Constable:** Israel would be victorious in battle — the opposite of what Balak wanted to hear. — Constable; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-23.html

---

## vv. 25–26 — Balak's Second Disappointment

### v. 25 — "Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!"

- Balak was frustrated: "If you can't curse them, at least don't bless them!" — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

### v. 26 — "Did I not tell you that whatever the LORD says, I must do?"

- Balaam could not shape God's message to please his audience. His commitment to faithfully report God's word is an example that many preachers today should learn from, even though his motives were corrupt. — Enduring Word; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-23/

---

## vv. 27–30 — Third Relocation to Peor

### v. 27 — "Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there."

- **Balak now says "Elohim":** He appears satisfied that Balaam was hindered by God (not by Balaam's unwillingness) from cursing Israel. Or the words may be spoken ironically. — Ellicott (from search excerpt); https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/23.htm

### v. 28 — "to the top of Peor, which overlooks the wasteland"

- **Peor:** This location becomes tragically significant in Numbers 25, where Israel sins with Moabite women at Baal-Peor. — Implicit connection noted by multiple commentators.

### vv. 29–30 — Third set of seven altars

- The third repetition of the seven-altar ritual. Balak's persistence in trying to manipulate God contrasts sharply with God's sovereign immutability declared in v. 19. The chapter ends on a cliffhanger, with the results of this third attempt awaiting Numbers 24.

- **Sailhamer (cited by Constable):** "Like Pharaoh before him, Balak also made three attempts to thwart God's blessing for Israel … and each attempt was turned into a blessing." — Constable; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-23.html

---

## Cross-Tradition Distinctives

**Reformed (Calvin, Piper):** Emphasis falls on God's sovereign immutability and unconditional election. v. 19 is the key text — God's decrees are unchangeable. Even Balaam's prophecy serves to "promulgate the covenant" to foreign nations. God uses corrupt instruments for His glory without endorsing their methods.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasis on the power of blessing vs. curse, the reality of spiritual warfare (sorcery and divination are real but powerless against God's people), and the danger of separating a "righteous death" from a righteous life. Application is strongly personal and devotional.

**Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon):** Gill stresses God's faithfulness to His promises and the literal fulfilment of prophecy regarding Israel. Spurgeon (cited in Enduring Word) draws the evangelistic point about the vanity of mere desires without a changed life.

**Evangelical/Dispensational (Constable, DTS):** Attention to the Abrahamic covenant promises being reaffirmed, the literal population growth of Israel, and the parallel with Pharaoh's three attempts to thwart blessing. Constable carefully distinguishes God's "larger purposes" (which do not change) from His responsive adjustments to human actions.

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes, cited by Precept Austin):**
- Notes that the sacrifices are pagan actions contrasting with true worship. The number seven was held in high regard among Semitic peoples generally; the many animals would provide abundant liver and organ materials for the diviner. — Precept Austin; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-23-commentary

**Catholic/Orthodox:** No results were retrievable from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search limits.
